html:
Okoumé is a tall tree of the Gabon forest whose light wood is ideal for plywood; from the 1890s until oil it was the main export of colonial Gabon.

European firms floated logs down the Ogooué river to the coast, and Port-Gentil grew as the timber port. Demand rose fast after the First World War as plywood spread. Labour was often forced, and the logging camps drew men away from farms and villages.

Timber made Gabon one of the few profitable parts of French Equatorial Africa before 1950. After independence it was overtaken by oil, but logging went on, and in 2010 Gabon banned the export of raw logs to build a wood industry at home. Its large remaining forest is now a base for conservation and carbon deals near Lambaréné and elsewhere.
sum: Okoumé is a tall tree of the Gabon forest whose light wood is ideal for plywood; from the 1890s until oil it was the main export of colonial Gabon.
